content: 1. The studies presented moderate heterogeneity, with an inconsistency measure (I²) of 16%. No downgrading was applied as the point estimates were similar, and the confidence intervals overlapped. 2. Two trials were excluded from the meta-analysis because they reported within-group change scores. Huang (2019) included 46 participants and was rated as having an overall low risk of bias. No significant differences were observed between groups for mean change from baseline. Kong (2020) included 121 participants and was rated as having an overall high risk of bias. Similarly, no statistically significant differences were found between groups for mean change from baseline. 3. Cho (2013) included 130 participants and was rated as having an overall unclear risk of bias. No serious events were reported, but 10 minor to moderate adverse events occurred in the acupuncture group, including pain and bruising at the acupuncture site. Haake (2007) included 774 participants and was rated as having an overall low risk of bias. No significant differences were observed between groups. Molsberger (2002) included 186 participants and was rated as having an overall high risk of bias. No important adverse events or side effects were observed in any group. 30. Minor adverse events were reported in several studies. Brinkhaus (2006) reported hematoma and bleeding in both groups. Cherkin (2009) reported mostly short-term pain with acupuncture, with one participant experiencing pain lasting one month. Huang (2019) reported subcutaneous hematoma after acupuncture. Kong (2020) reported minor pain, bruising, skin rash, and slight bleeding at the needle site, as well as mild reactions to the prone position, including nausea, dizziness, and mild backache. Koppenhaver (2021) reported pain during treatment, dizziness, and unspecified emotional changes. Yuan (2016) reported transient worsening of back pain, acupuncture point bruising, back and leg numbness, discomfort, and shoulder pain lasting up to one week. 31.
